what_it_does: Modern data centers increasingly attach extra memory to servers via CXL (Compute Express Link — a fast, standardized cable/interface that lets a CPU treat a remote memory device almost like local memory). When this is done inside a confidential-computing environment — a walled-off area where even the cloud operator cannot read your data, created by features like Intel TDX or AMD SEV — the data flowing over that link must be encrypted at the page level. The industry standard for this is XTS encryption (a block-cipher mode designed for storage, applied here per memory page), but XTS adds noticeable slowdown. AIORE addresses this by classifying pages as 'hot' (frequently accessed) or 'cold' (rarely accessed): hot pages use a faster, more parallelizable encryption mode (CTR mode), while cold pages stay in the slower but standards-compliant XTS. When a page's temperature changes, only that page is re-encrypted rather than the whole memory region, and the re-encryption work is done by compute resources inside the CXL memory device itself — so it overlaps with normal memory traffic and hides most of the latency cost.
